title: The one-drop flip: titrating HCl with NaOH

intent.goal: Show why a titration's end point is so sharp: one drop moves the pH by more than five units.
intent.audience: Students aged 15 to 20 and curious adults; US and European English.
intent.takeaway: Near the equivalence point there is almost no acid left to resist the base, so one drop flips the solution.
intent.hook: A colourless flask turns pink from a single drop.
emotional_arc: tension as the curve stays flat

science.model: complete dissociation, ideal solution, additive volumes, 25 °C
caveats: Activities are taken equal to concentrations.
One drop is taken as 0.05 mL.
The pink of the indicator is drawn across its cited colour-change range; it is a display mapping, not a spectrum.

music.note: Sample style is music only; the text carries the lesson.

sfx: low swell at the colour change

camera.moves: slow push from the whole apparatus to the flask, then a pull back; no cuts

timeline.visual: Whole apparatus: burette on a stand over a conical flask, two reagent bottles. Title appears.
Labels with leader lines for the burette and the flask. Card shows the neutralisation equation.

timeline.purpose: Build tension: lots of base, almost no change.
timeline.visual: Drops fall, the burette level sinks, the flask fills. Card draws the computed pH curve with a moving dot. Camera pushes in.
One drop hangs, falls, and the flask turns pink. The dot on the curve jumps. Label for the indicator.

timeline.purpose: The reason, in one line of maths.
timeline.visual: Camera pulls back to the pink flask. Card shows the equivalence-point formula and the model note.

c1_note.text: Equal moles of acid and base leave only salt and water.

c2_heading.text: 2. The pH hardly moves… until the end

c3_note.text: About {1|250 000 times} fewer H⁺ ions, from 0.05 mL of base

c4_note.text: Moles of base added = moles of acid. Model: ideal solution at 25 °C.
